message: The measurements point clearly at an interpretable model, so I'm committing to a glass-box rubric rather than racing several families. There are only 42 rows per input, which is under the floor a neural model needs, and the strongest single input explains 41% of the answer — well within the leakage ceiling, so nothing looks like the answer in disguise. I ruled out gradient boosting: it would likely score slightly higher, but the team needs to see exactly why each member was scored, and a rubric gives that exactly.
reasoning: Read the gate reports first (MLP inadmissible on rows-per-feature), weighed the interpretability requirement against a marginal metric gain, and committed rather than deferring because the evidence separates the candidates cleanly.

Architecture.Rationale: Interpretability is the stated requirement and the data is thin (42 rows per input). A glass-box rubric gives an exact per-record explanation of every score, which is what the team will act on, and nothing in the statistics suggests a stronger family would be justified here.

Candidates.Rationale: Every score decomposes into named, weighted inputs, so a member's result can be explained line by line. Passed all gates.
